title: On the bike
note: Fictional patients. Eligibility and stop rules are agreed with the nephrologist and head nurse; the nurse checks pressure and you never touch the machine or lines.
intro: You are the physical therapist running the new intradialytic exercise program on the morning shift. Two pedal cycles are available. Today’s list has Mr. Felipe Ramos, 66, who had a drop in blood pressure in the chair last Wednesday, and Mrs. Carmen Velasco, 61, who has done six sessions without problems.

choices.text: Not today: the agreed rules exclude recent hypotension in the chair.
choices.feedback: Eligibility is agreed in advance with the nephrologist and head nurse, per unit protocol: stable sessions and no recent hypotension in the chair.

choices.text: Let him cycle at a lower resistance for a shorter time, with the nurse checking his pressure more often.
choices.feedback: A lighter load still adds to the strain of fluid removal. The agreed rule excludes him for now.
choices.then: The nurse reminds you of the rule. Mrs. Velasco cycles today.

choices.text: Ask him whether he feels up to it.
choices.feedback: His view matters, but the eligibility rule is clinical, agreed with the team. Check it first.
choices.then: The rule excludes him for now. Mrs. Velasco cycles today.

n2.prompt: When does Mrs. Velasco start cycling?

choices.text: After a smooth connection, in the agreed slot in the first half.
choices.feedback: Exercise in the first half of the session. Nurses are busiest at connection and disconnection; a fixed slot after connection keeps the program from depending on them at those times.

choices.text: Straight away, while the nurse is connecting, to save time.
choices.feedback: Connection needs the nurse’s full attention, and the session should be running smoothly first.
choices.then: You wait until 08:10, after the nurse confirms she is stable.

choices.text: In the last hour, when she has settled into the session and the nurse has more time to watch her.
choices.feedback: The last hour is when fluid removal has gone furthest and blood pressure is most likely to fall. Use the first half.

n3.prompt: How do you set her up on the bike?

choices.text: Legs only, fistula arm still and visible, lines clear; warm up, then RPE 11 to 13.
choices.feedback: The access arm must stay still and in view, and the lines clear of moving parts. RPE 11 to 13 is “fairly light” to “somewhat hard,” progressing toward 30 minutes over weeks.

choices.text: Cover her arm with a light blanket to keep her warm while she cycles, and start at a moderate pace.
choices.feedback: The access arm stays visible during exercise, so any needle movement or bleeding is seen at once.
choices.then: You fold the blanket back so the arm is in view.

choices.text: Start at a hard pace to make the most of the time.
choices.feedback: Start with a warm-up and a moderate effort. A hard pace early raises the risk of a drop in pressure and makes people stop coming.
choices.then: You ease her to RPE 12 after a warm-up.

n4.scene: Twenty minutes into cycling she starts yawning and says she feels a little sick.

choices.text: Stop pedaling and call the nurse at once.
choices.feedback: Yawning and nausea can be the first signs of a falling blood pressure. Stop and call; the nurse checks the pressure and responds. You never touch the machine or lines.
choices.then: The nurse finds 96/58, reclines the chair, and adjusts treatment. Mrs. Velasco recovers within minutes.

choices.text: Lower the resistance and let her keep going slowly, since gentle movement helps return blood to the heart.
choices.feedback: Any symptom means stop. Pedaling on can deepen a falling pressure.
choices.then: She becomes pale. You stop and call the nurse, who reclines the chair and manages it.

choices.text: Pause the fluid removal on the machine yourself while you call the nurse.
choices.feedback: You never touch the machine or lines. Stop the exercise and call the nurse; treatment changes are hers.
choices.then: The nurse arrives, manages the pressure, and reminds you of the rule.

n5.scene: When she is settled, Mrs. Velasco asks: “Will this make me live longer?”

choices.text: Stronger and fewer hospital days in studies; no proof yet of a longer life.
choices.feedback: The DiaTT trial improved sit-to-stand performance and found fewer hospital days as a secondary finding, with no effect on mortality. An honest answer builds trust.

choices.text: “Yes. People who exercise live longer, and that is why we are starting this program for you.”
choices.feedback: No trial in dialysis has shown that. Overpromising damages trust when the promise is not kept.
Many people do feel better, but answer her actual question: what is shown, and what is not yet known.

end.title: Three months on
end.text: You record the stopped session and the nurse’s response. The program tracks sessions offered and done, and sit-to-stand every three months. Mrs. Velasco’s sit-to-stand count rises from 12 to 15. Mr. Ramos joins once the nephrologist confirms his sessions are stable again.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Eligibility and stop rules are agreed in advance with the nephrologist and head nurse.
  • Exercise in the first half, after a smooth connection, in a fixed slot.
  • Access arm still and visible, lines clear of the pedals.
  • Any symptom: stop and call the nurse. Never touch the machine or lines.
  • Answer honestly about what the trials show.

See Setting up safely, The trials and Measuring the program.
